concepts.name: Reversing a linked list by re-pointing `next`
The dummy head node (Merge Two Sorted Lists)
Floyd's cycle detection with slow and fast pointers
Reorder List: find the middle, reverse, merge

questions.prompt:
What should this iterative reversal return in place of `???`

```python
def reverse(head):
    prev = None
    cur = head
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev = cur
        cur = nxt
    return ???
```

choices.text: `cur`
`head`
`prev`
`nxt`

questions.explanation: The loop ends when `cur` is `None`, and at that point `prev` is the last node of the original list, which is the head of the reversed one. `head` is still the original first node, which is now the tail with `next = None`. Returning `cur` or `nxt` returns `None`.

questions.prompt: A learner drops the `nxt` variable and writes the loop body as `cur.next = prev; prev = cur; cur = cur.next`. What does `reverse` now return for `1 -> 2 -> 3`?

choices.text: `3 -> 2 -> 1`, because the order of assignments doesn't matter
Just `1`: the rest is lost because `cur.next` was overwritten before moving on
It never returns, because the loop keeps cycling between two nodes
It raises `AttributeError` because `cur` becomes `None` too early

questions.explanation: After `cur.next = prev`, the only link to node 2 is gone, and `cur = cur.next` moves to `prev`, which is `None` on the first pass. The loop stops after one step and returns the single node `1`. Saving `nxt = cur.next` before re-pointing is the whole trick. Drawing the three pointers on paper, as the exercise asks, shows this at once.

questions.prompt: Explain how to reverse a singly linked list iteratively, and compare its time and space cost with a recursive version.

model_answer.summary: Walk the list once with `prev` and `cur`, saving `cur.next` before pointing it back at `prev`. It takes O(n) time and O(1) extra space; recursion also takes O(n) time but uses O(n) stack.
key_points: Each step: save `nxt = cur.next`, set `cur.next = prev`, then advance `prev = cur` and `cur = nxt`
When `cur` is `None`, `prev` is the new head
Iterative: O(n) time, O(1) extra space
Recursive: also O(n) time, but O(n) call stack, which in Python hits the default recursion limit (1000) on long lists

questions.explanation: LeetCode's Reverse Linked List allows up to 5,000 nodes, which is deeper than CPython's default recursion limit of 1000, so the iterative version is the safer default in Python.

questions.prompt: Why do most solutions to Merge Two Sorted Lists start with a dummy node, `dummy = ListNode()` and `tail = dummy`?

choices.text: It keeps the merge O(log n) instead of O(n), since fewer nodes are walked
It stores the combined length of the two lists for the final loop
It means the first values never have to be compared before the loop
No special case for the head: always attach to `tail.next`, return `dummy.next`

questions.explanation: Without a dummy you need special code to pick the head of the result before the loop starts. With one, every node, including the first, is attached the same way with `tail.next = node`, and the real head is `dummy.next`. The merge is still O(n + m), and values are compared on every step as usual.

questions.prompt: In Merge Two Sorted Lists, the loop `while l1 and l2:` ends. What must happen next?

choices.text: Nothing: the loop has already attached every node from both lists
Attach whichever list is left over in one step: `tail.next = l1 or l2`
Walk the leftover list and attach its nodes one at a time, comparing each with `None`
Reverse the leftover list, then attach it to `tail`

questions.explanation: The loop stops as soon as one list runs out, and the other may still hold nodes. They are already sorted and all at least as large as everything merged so far, so one pointer attaches the whole remainder. Forgetting this step silently drops the tail of the longer list. Walking the remainder node by node works but does pointless extra work.

questions.prompt: Explain how to merge two sorted linked lists by splicing their nodes, using a dummy head. Give the time and extra space.

model_answer.summary: Use a dummy node and a `tail` pointer; repeatedly attach the smaller of the two current nodes and advance, then attach whatever remains, and return `dummy.next`. It takes O(n + m) time and O(1) extra space.
key_points: Create a dummy node and set `tail = dummy`
While both lists have nodes, attach the smaller head to `tail.next`, advance that list, and advance `tail`
Attach the non-empty remainder with `tail.next = l1 or l2`
O(n + m) time, O(1) extra space, because it re-links existing nodes instead of creating new ones

questions.explanation: The problem says the list should be made by splicing together the nodes of the two lists, so the solution moves pointers rather than copying values. The dummy node removes the empty-result special case.

questions.prompt: In Floyd's cycle detection, `slow` moves one node per step and `fast` moves two. What tells you the list has a cycle?

choices.text: `slow` and `fast` point to the same node
`fast` reaches `None`
`slow.val == fast.val`
`fast` passes the head node a second time

questions.explanation: If there is a cycle, both pointers end up going round it and `fast` catches up with `slow`, so `slow is fast` for the same node. If `fast` reaches `None` there is no cycle. Comparing values is wrong because different nodes can hold equal values. The cycle may not include the head, so `fast` might never pass it again.

questions.prompt: What extra space does Floyd's algorithm use, compared with storing every visited node in a `set`?

choices.text: Both use O(n), because both must remember visited nodes
Floyd uses O(log n), the set uses O(n)
Floyd uses O(1), the set uses O(n)
Both use O(1), since the set only stores references

questions.explanation: Floyd keeps just two pointers, so it needs O(1) extra space, which is what the problem's follow-up asks for. A visited set grows by one reference per node, which is O(n): references are small, but there are n of them. Both approaches run in O(n) time.

questions.prompt: Explain why, in a list with a cycle, a fast pointer moving two steps is guaranteed to meet a slow pointer moving one step, rather than jumping over it forever.

model_answer.summary: Once both pointers are in the cycle, the distance from `fast` forward to `slow` shrinks by exactly one node per step, so it must reach zero. In a list without a cycle, `fast` reaches the end instead.
key_points: `slow` eventually enters the cycle, and `fast` is already in it
Each step, `fast` moves 2 and `slow` moves 1, so the gap between them closes by exactly 1
A gap that shrinks by 1 each step can't skip past 0, so they land on the same node
They meet within one lap of `slow` around the cycle
Without a cycle, `fast` hits `None`, so the loop checks `fast and fast.next` before stepping

questions.explanation: The key is relative speed. Measured from `slow`, `fast` approaches one node at a time, so it can't leap over. That's why the speeds are 1 and 2 rather than, say, 1 and 3.

questions.prompt: Reorder List turns `L0 → L1 → … → Ln` into `L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln-1 → …`. Which plan runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra space?

choices.text: For each node, walk to the current tail, unlink it and insert it after that node
Copy the values into an array, then write them back in the new order
Find the middle with slow and fast pointers, reverse the second half, then merge the halves alternately
Sort the nodes by their position from the end, then relink them

questions.explanation: Slow/fast finds the middle in one pass, reversing the second half is another pass, and merging alternately is a third: O(n) time, O(1) space. Walking to the tail for every node is O(n²). Copying values uses O(n) space, and the problem says you may not modify the values, only the nodes.

questions.prompt: What does Reorder List produce for `1 → 2 → 3 → 4`?
questions.explanation: The pattern is first, last, second, second-to-last, and so on: `1, 4, 2, 3`. In the three-step plan the halves are `1 → 2` and `3 → 4`; reversing the second gives `4 → 3`, and merging alternately gives `1 → 4 → 2 → 3`.
